Adolph F. Bandelier compiled a documentary history of the Rio Grande Pueblos of New Mexico. Part one gives a bibliographic introduction to the sources. Bandelier was a pioneering scholar of the Southwest's peoples.

The region's geography, he says, is too well known to need mention. Folklore and tradition, though, carry decisive importance in many cases. He touches them only when the sources themselves allude to them. That discipline marks the work as documentary, not legendary. Bandelier lets Spanish records speak for the Pueblo past. Readers get the paper trail of missions, pueblos, and colonial rule. It remains a foundation work for historians of the Rio Grande valley.
22542-jesus-the-christ-a-study-of-the-me:
James E. Talmage wrote Jesus the Christ, a study of the Messiah and His mission. It follows ancient and modern scripture, per its subtitle. Talmage wrote it for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

He entered the work under appointment from presiding church authorities. The completed book was read to the First Presidency for approval. The Council of the Twelve also reviewed and approved it. Yet it presents, he stresses, his personal belief and conviction. Talmage traces Christ's life from premortal existence to resurrection. Each event is weighed against scripture, history, and doctrine in detail. The book became a standard Latter-day Saint reference. Readers get systematic theology joined to a life of Christ.
